e.t: This adjective means “pure,” describing something clean, unmixed, or free from defilement. It is a quality word rather than the name of an object, so its exact emphasis depends on what it describes in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Leviticus, Job, and Psalms. Its sense remains centered on purity, whether referring to something presented, encountered, or described. The word belongs specifically to the Greek Old Testament tradition and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament lexical entry.

This word is a proper name referring to a person named Adōnia, also rendered Athonia. It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Kings and once in 1 Chronicles. The English renderings preserve it as Adonias or Adonia, reflecting its use as a name. Its precise reference is identified by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This noun means “prizefighter,” referring to a person who competes in fighting for a prize. It is used three times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in 4 Maccabees. The word presents its subject as a disciplined competitor engaged in a contest, rather than simply describing ordinary physical strength. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a fighter competing for victory and reward.

This adjective describes someone as modest or shamefaced—reserved and conscious of proper conduct. It presents a person whose manner is marked by modesty rather than bold self-display. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX material, all in Sirach, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. One recorded English rendering is “shamefaced.”

This word means “upheaval,” describing a state of disturbance, instability, or disorder. As a noun, it refers to the condition itself rather than to an action someone performs. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 33:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains a situation thrown into confusion or lacking settled order.

This verb means “make false pretensions”: to present oneself as more important, capable, or worthy than is true. It describes a person’s self-promoting claim or boast rather than a simple statement of fact. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea remains pretending to possess a status or greatness one does not truly have.

This Greek LXX noun means “change” or “alteration”: a difference produced when something becomes otherwise than it was. It names the change itself rather than describing the action as a verb. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Psalms and three times in Sirach. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a transition, modification, or changed condition. It is rendered “change” where an English rendering is available. [P03 identity; P03 occurrences]

Amphin (also called Amfin) is a proper name, not a word that describes an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the LXX and appears only once in that corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:15. The available information gives the name itself but does not provide a separate lexical definition or a verse description. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding genealogical context.

This Greek LXX noun means “examination”: a careful inquiry or inspection carried out to understand or assess something. In biblical usage, it functions as a name for that kind of investigative process, rather than describing the person who examines or the conclusion reached. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:5, so the surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which the examination is mentioned.

This Greek LXX verb means “bring forth again.” It describes an act of producing, giving birth, or bringing something forth once more, depending on the sentence. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 16:13. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its exact force in that occurrence cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains the repeated bringing forth of something, expressed as an action rather than as a person, object, or quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “threat”: an expression or prospect of harm intended to cause fear or pressure. It names the danger held over someone rather than the act of threatening itself. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it can describe threatening speech or an intimidating danger in different settings. Its basic sense remains a warning of harm, whether the threat comes from a person, a ruler, or surrounding circumstances.

This word means “on the lookout,” describing someone who is watching attentively and staying alert. It functions as a verb, expressing the act of keeping watch rather than merely possessing awareness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:30. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is active attentiveness—watching for something or remaining alert to what may happen.

Arachi, also rendered Arakhi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs three times, all within 2 Samuel 17:5, 17:14, and 17:15. Because those passages are referenced without their verse text here, the name’s precise role in each sentence cannot be explained further. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal designation Arachi or Arakhi.

Aretas is a personal name, not a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs seven times as a proper name. Its appearances are concentrated especially in Isaiah, with additional occurrences in Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The name itself identifies a person, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine which person and what is being said about him.

This Greek LXX noun means “breakfast,” the meal eaten early in the day. It names a meal rather than an action, person, or quality. The word appears four times in this LXX corpus: twice in Old Testament books and twice in Bel and the Dragon. Its basic meaning remains straightforward wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse determines what is said about that meal. Scripture references for its occurrences include 2 Samuel 24:15, 1 Kings 2:46, and Bel and the Dragon 1:34 and 1:37.

Asabdana, also rendered Asavthana, is a proper name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, in Nehemiah 8:4, and its precise significance is not defined by the name itself. The available form preserves the person’s designation without providing an English meaning or further lexical explanation.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Asouphe” or “Asufe.” It identifies a person or family name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:43. The available information establishes its naming function and accepted forms, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or group named there.

This word means “bitumen,” a noun naming a material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 2:3. The word itself identifies the material rather than an action, person, or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the material called bitumen. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

Achamani, also rendered Akhamani, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation. This name occurs twice in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, appearing in 1 Chronicles 11:11 and 27:32. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity and role cannot be described further; the word itself functions as the person’s name.

Baithmarchabōth, also rendered Vethmarkhavoth, is a proper name. It identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea; the available information does not specify which kind of entity it names. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:31. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from that passage and its surrounding context.

gl: weighed down: to be heavy at heart
d: weighed down: to be heavy at heart

e.t: This verb means “weighed down: to be heavy at heart,” describing a person burdened inwardly by distress or discouragement. It presents heaviness of heart as an experienced condition rather than naming an outward weight. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers and 1 Kings, so its normal sense is clear, while its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It expresses emotional oppression or troubled feeling.

This noun means “violence”—force or harmful action used against others. It names violent conduct rather than describing a person or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 28 times, showing that the word is used across accounts of oppression, conflict, and destructive power. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the use of force that causes harm or injustice.

This proper name refers to the Gabaonites, also rendered Gavaonitis. It identifies a people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs seven times, appearing mainly in 2 Samuel 21 and once in 1 Chronicles 12. Its repeated use as a people’s name helps readers recognize that references to the Gabaonites concern a distinct group within Israel’s historical account.

The word is a proper name for “Galaaditis,” also given as “Galaathitis.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action word. In the LXX corpus, it occurs five times: three times in Joshua and Amos, and twice in 1 Maccabees. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent in each passage cannot be stated more specifically.

Gedsour, also rendered Yethsur, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs seven times across seven verses in the LXX corpus, appearing in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. The exact person or place intended in any particular verse must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not a broader abstract meaning.

This noun means a “stile for writing,” a pointed instrument used to mark or inscribe words. It names a physical writing tool rather than the act of writing or the message written. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Exodus, 1 Kings, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains a tool used for writing or engraving.

This word describes someone or something that is ten months old. It functions as a noun referring to a person or thing by that age, rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:7. The available meaning is precise, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the word itself should be understood simply as an age designation: ten months old.

gl: endure to the end; last out
d: endure to the end; last out

e.t: This verb means to endure to the end or to last out. It describes continuing firmly until something is completed or a difficult period has passed, rather than giving up partway through. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:9. Its basic meaning emphasizes persistence and staying power, but the exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means to go through or pass through, describing movement from one side, place, or point to another. It focuses on the act of proceeding through something rather than simply arriving or remaining. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once each in Judges, 2 Samuel, Job, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what person or thing is moving and what it passes through.

This word means an “administrator” or “steward,” describing someone entrusted with managing affairs, resources, or responsibilities. It is a noun for a person who oversees an appointed task or sphere of service. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Ezra and once in Daniel, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse texts are not included here. The word points to responsible oversight rather than merely ordinary labor or attendance.

This Greek word means “able” or “can”: it expresses having the power, capacity, or permission to do something. As a verb, it describes what a person or group is capable of doing, whether the ability is present, possible, or granted. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 288 times, showing that Scripture uses it broadly for questions of capability and possibility. The precise force in any passage depends on what action or situation accompanies it, but its central idea remains the ability to act.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Dōdai” or “Thothe.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:12. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself tells us chiefly whom the passage names, not the person’s role or significance in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal designation preserved in the Greek rendering of the Old Testament.

gl: affect deafness; pretend not to hear
d: affect deafness; pretend not to hear

e.t: This verb means to affect deafness—to pretend not to hear. It describes a deliberate refusal to listen, rather than an inability to hear. In its one recorded occurrence in the Greek LXX corpus, the word appears in Sirach 19:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to someone acting as though they cannot hear in order to avoid receiving or responding to what is said.

This LXX verb means “pick out of a cohort.” It describes selecting one person from a larger company or group, emphasizing the act of singling someone out rather than treating the group as a whole. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition, in Song of Songs 5:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

Eleazaros is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning in the Greek LXX corpus is represented by the name “Eleazaros.” It appears 16 times, across 16 verses, in the deuterocanonical writings, including 1–3 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. The name itself does not provide enough information to identify which person is intended in any particular passage; that requires the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This adjective means “afraid,” describing someone who feels fear or is in a fearful state. It identifies a person as frightened rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 19:24. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what caused the fear or how the word functions in that passage; its basic meaning remains a description of being afraid.

Enak is a proper name referring to a person named Enak in the Greek Old Testament. Unlike an ordinary word that describes an action, quality, or object, this term identifies an individual. It appears seven times across six verses, from Deuteronomy through Judges. The name occurs in passages connected with Israel’s inheritance and the people of the land, but its precise significance in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding text.

This noun means “prominence,” referring to a place or position that stands out above or beyond what surrounds it. It describes distinction by elevation or visible position rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 39:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the idea of being raised, noticeable, or set apart in position.

This Greek LXX adverb means “tomorrow” or “next day.” It points to the day immediately following the present day or the day currently being discussed. The word can mark when something will happen, when an action is expected, or when a time period reaches its following day. It occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Samuel, and Judges. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective describes something as “likely”—something expected or regarded as probable. It expresses possibility with a reasonable expectation, rather than certainty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Daniel. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the idea of what is likely or probable.

This Greek LXX noun means “clouded” or “dark.” It describes something marked by obscurity or a lack of brightness, giving the reader the basic sense of a dim or overcast condition. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 1:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary lexical idea remains one of cloudiness or darkness.

This LXX adverb means “ready,” describing someone or something prepared to act, respond, or be used without delay. It presents readiness as a condition of preparedness rather than naming the action itself. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing three times in Ezra and once in Daniel. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding passage says is ready and what is expected to follow.

This adjective means “annual,” describing something that happens or is observed once each year. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 15:18. Because the word occurs only once and the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains a yearly or once-a-year designation.

Ziph is a proper name, also rendered Zif. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not establish whether each occurrence refers to a person, place, or another named subject. The word occurs six times in five Old Testament verses, from 1 Samuel through 2 Chronicles, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage, while its basic lexical function is simply to name Ziph or Zif.

This noun means an “inner room”—a room set farther inside a house or building, rather than an open or outer area. It can refer to a private interior space, though the precise use in a passage depends on the surrounding wording. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:18. The word itself identifies the kind of place being mentioned; the verse context supplies its particular role.

Tharseas is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint corpus represented here), it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 3:5. The name itself identifies the individual, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role or significance in the account. No broader lexical sense is indicated for this name.

This noun refers to a hunt or to game—the wild animals pursued or taken in hunting. It describes the activity of hunting and, depending on the sentence, the animal obtained through it. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 29 times, with uses extending from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. Its ordinary meaning remains centered on hunting and hunted animals rather than on a broader idea of pursuit or conflict.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Iesoui” or “Iesoi.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:28. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated here. Its basic function is clear: it serves as a proper name for a person.

Ιωαδιν is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is represented as “Iōadin” and “Ioathin.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:2. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes one individual from others named in the surrounding historical record. The precise role of the named person depends on the verse and its wider context.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iōnathēs” or “Ionathis.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in 1 Maccabees 2:5 and once in 2 Maccabees 8:22. Because the word functions as a proper name, its significance in either passage depends on which person bears the name and on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX conjunction means “although.” It introduces a statement that contrasts with, or qualifies, the main statement, marking something as true despite another circumstance. As a connecting word, it does not name a person, object, or action; instead, it shows how one thought relates to another. It occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, including Proverbs, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees.

This noun means “patient endurance” or “patience”: the steady ability to remain firm and continue faithfully through difficulty. It describes perseverance that does not give up when suffering, pressure, or opposition persists. The word appears six times in the Greek LXX material represented here, all in 4 Maccabees, where its repeated use highlights endurance as a sustained quality rather than a brief moment of courage.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead down” or “draw up,” describing the act of bringing or guiding someone or something from one place to another. Its basic sense concerns directed movement, with the surrounding passage determining whether the movement is downward or upward in the particular sentence. The word occurs 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so it is a regularly used action word rather than a rare expression. It appears across historical, poetic, and wisdom books, including Genesis, Kings, Psalms, Lamentations, and Sirach.

This verb means to speak against someone—to oppose or testify negatively against them. It describes speech directed contrary to a person or claim, rather than ordinary conversation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 14:37, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as an action: someone voices opposition through speech. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek Old Testament word means “steal”: to take what belongs to another person without permission. It is a verb describing an action, whether the object taken is property or something otherwise guarded. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, including laws that forbid stealing and narratives involving suspected or actual theft. Its basic meaning remains direct and consistent: secretly or unlawfully taking another person’s possession. The surrounding passage determines the specific object and circumstances, but the word itself names the act of stealing.

This word means “meat,” referring to the flesh of an animal used as food. It is a noun describing physical nourishment rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 85 times, especially in passages concerning eating, shared meals, and sacrificial food. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: animal flesh prepared, eaten, or otherwise discussed as food. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “of a swan,” describing something connected with or belonging to a swan. It is a specific descriptive word rather than a general term for a bird or animal. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:21. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes there, but the word’s basic meaning remains a reference to a swan.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “handle of an oar,” the part of an oar that a person grips to move or guide a vessel. It names a tangible tool rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 27:6. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The term therefore points to a specific physical implement used in rowing.

gl: hollow on each side below the ribs; flank
d: hollow on each side below the ribs; flank

e.h: A Flank or Side of the Body
e.t: This noun means the hollow area on each side of the body below the ribs—the flank. It names a specific part of human anatomy rather than an action, feeling, or spiritual quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 47:19. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the bodily area beside the lower ribs.

This Greek LXX verb means “stone”: to attack someone by throwing stones. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel 16, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This noun means “letting loose,” referring to the act of releasing something rather than keeping it held. It names an action or condition, while the surrounding passage identifies what is being released and why. In this LXX corpus, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Ecclesiastes, Daniel, and Wisdom. These occurrences show that the word is used across several biblical books, but the available information supports its basic sense without adding a more specific meaning.

This noun refers to a woollen cloak, a piece of outer clothing worn over other garments. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a recognizable item of clothing rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs six times across six Old Testament verses, including passages in Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a woollen cloak or covering garment.

This noun means “middle,” referring to a position between two sides, points, or extremes. It identifies an intermediate place or position rather than an end or beginning. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:18. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its basic sense remains a central or intervening position.

This word means “form,” referring to the visible or recognizable shape, appearance, or configuration of something. As a noun, it identifies what something looks like or the form it takes rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Job, Isaiah, Daniel, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person, object, or condition is being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “hamstring.” It describes the act of hamstringing, a physical action expressed as a verb rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the disabling action identified by the term “hamstring.”

This verb means “adulterate”: to make something impure or less genuine by altering or mixing it with something inferior. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 14:24, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its lexical sense remains the act of adulterating or corrupting what should be genuine.

This Greek LXX verb means “destroy”: to ruin, kill, or bring something to an end so that it no longer remains or functions as before. It is used 17 times across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Exodus, Joshua, Judges, Jeremiah, and later writings. The word describes decisive destruction, whether directed against a person, a group, or something that must be removed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: at what point of time; at what hour
d: at what point of time; at what hour

e.h: A Word for At What Hour
e.t: This word means “at what hour”. It asks about the time when something occurs, rather than naming the event itself. As an adverb, it functions as a question about timing and may also express “at what point of time” when that wording better fits the sentence. It occurs once in the Greek LXX material, with the sole reference listed as 4 Maccabees 2:21. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise use in that sentence must be understood from its context.

The word means “fowl”: it names a bird or birds as a noun. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 33 times, so it is a recurring everyday term rather than a rare technical expression. It appears in passages ranging from Genesis and Deuteronomy to Proverbs and later writings. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun describes someone or something marked by suffering or mourning. It presents a sorrowful, afflicted condition rather than an action or command. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 29:25, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central sense remains clear: it points to what is painful, sorrowful, or mournful.

This adverb describes an action done unlawfully or wickedly—that is, in a way contrary to what is right or permitted. It tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Proverbs, showing its use as a concise description of wrongful conduct. The surrounding verse determines what specific act is being characterized, but the word itself points to behavior marked by lawlessness or wickedness.

This verb means to “further annoy”—to continue irritating or troubling someone. It describes added disturbance rather than a first, isolated irritation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, it occurs 13 times, so it is a recurring word for continued vexation or trouble. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the continuation of annoyance.

This noun refers to “that which is trodden”—something pressed or walked upon. It describes a surface or material marked by the action of being stepped on, rather than the person doing the treading. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Kings 19:26 and Ezekiel 34:19. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of what has been trampled or used underfoot.

This Greek LXX noun means “enclosure”: a bounded or enclosed space. It can refer generally to an area set apart by surrounding walls or boundaries, rather than to the wall or boundary itself. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for a defined physical space. Its exact reference—such as a building area, courtyard, or other bounded place—depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “error.” It names a mistake or a course of being wrong, rather than describing the person who is mistaken. In this LXX corpus, it occurs five times in five verses, appearing in Proverbs, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. It can be rendered in either singular or plural according to the sentence, but its central idea remains error. The surrounding verse determines what kind of error is meant in each occurrence.

This LXX Greek word means “besides” or “only.” It can add something alongside what has already been mentioned, or restrict attention to one person or thing. As a conjunction, adverb, or preposition, its exact English expression depends on how it connects the surrounding words. It occurs 220 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, showing that it serves several connecting and limiting uses rather than describing a particular object or action. Its precise force in a verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “drink”—a liquid intended to be consumed. It names the beverage itself rather than the act of drinking. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, appearing once in Psalms and three times in the deuterocanonical books represented here. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a drink or beverage. The word is therefore straightforward: it refers to something taken as refreshment or nourishment by drinking.

This Greek LXX verb means “get close to.” It describes moving nearer to a person, place, object, or situation. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming the person or thing approached. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 12 verses, from Genesis through Daniel. Its basic sense remains straightforward: someone or something comes nearer. The exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being approached and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “anticipate” or “spring forth.” It describes coming before something else, either by acting ahead of it or by bursting forward. As a verb, it expresses movement or action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Job, Psalms, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Raphael is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be described here. The name itself remains a proper name rendered as “Raphael,” and its meaning does not function as a general term used throughout the passage.

Raphē is a proper name, referring to a person named Raphe or Rhafi rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles. The available wording supports the name itself, but does not provide an additional meaning or description of the person. Its significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding genealogy and verse text.

“Ruth” is a personal name referring to the woman named Ruth in the Greek Old Testament text. It functions as a noun and does not describe an action, quality, or general object. This name appears 19 times in the Greek text of Ruth, spanning 19 verses from Ruth 1:4 through Ruth 4:13. The word’s meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it points to a particular person rather than expressing a broader concept.

This Greek LXX noun means “eating flesh,” referring plainly to the act or practice of consuming flesh. It names an activity rather than a person, object, or quality. In this corpus, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees, at 5:8 and 5:14. The word’s basic meaning is specific and concrete; its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument. It should therefore be understood first as a description of flesh-eating, without adding a broader spiritual or moral meaning not stated by the passage.

Sarsousin, also rendered Sarsusin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once, in Joshua 19:5, within the boundary lists of Joshua. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it names a specific location, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that location.

Silo is a proper name for a place in the Old Testament. It is rendered as “Sēlō” or “Silo,” so it functions as a geographical name rather than a description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 13 times, beginning in Joshua and appearing later in 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Nehemiah. Several occurrences are in Joshua, including references to the place where Israel gathered and where territorial matters were addressed, though the word itself simply identifies Silo.

Sikimos is a proper name used in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a named person, place, or other particular referent in the passages where it appears, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of referent it is. The word occurs 20 times in the Septuagint corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion. Its exact significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “silence”: the absence or restraint of speech and sound. As a noun, it identifies a state or condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Amos and once in Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused and straightforward: quietness or silence. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to people being quiet, a quiet condition, or the absence of sound, but the word itself supplies the idea of silence.

This verb means “turn; turned around,” describing a change in direction or orientation. It can refer to something physically turning, or to a person or thing being turned from one position toward another. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 41 times, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is turning and the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “sign”: a mark or indication that points to something beyond itself. It can describe something recognized as meaningful or used to signify another reality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs three times—once in the Old Testament and twice in the deuterocanonical book of Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what the surrounding text identifies as the sign and what it points toward. The word itself names the sign, not necessarily the interpretation or purpose attached to it.

This verb means “burn up” or “parch,” describing something dried, scorched, or consumed by heat. It is a physical word for the effect of intense heat rather than a general expression for distress or difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented here, it occurs twice, including once in Psalms 101:4 and once in 4 Maccabees 3:11. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 8:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on pursuing and driving away in company with others.

This noun means “sensibility”: the capacity to think and respond with sound, balanced judgment. It describes a settled quality of mind rather than a single feeling or impulse. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears nine times, including several occurrences in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains thoughtful self-control and practical wisdom rather than rashness or excess.

Tatam is a proper name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entry in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 15:59. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise person or place identified by Tatam cannot be stated from this lexical information alone.

This Greek LXX noun means “craftsman,” referring to a person skilled in making or working with materials. It identifies someone whose ability is expressed through practical workmanship rather than merely naming an object or activity. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical books represented here, showing repeated use for skilled workers across several settings. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains a person who makes or shapes things through practiced skill.

This Greek LXX verb means “lift over/up.” It describes raising something or carrying it beyond or above a point, rather than simply leaving it in place. As a verb, it expresses an action performed by someone or something. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Psalms, Proverbs, 2 Chronicles, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being lifted and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “elevate/lift on high”—to raise something or someone upward or place it in a high position. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 37 times, appearing especially in Daniel and also in Psalms. Its wording can describe physical lifting, while its broader sense may express being raised or exalted; the surrounding verse determines which emphasis is intended. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

Phathaia, also rendered Fathea, is a proper name belonging to a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or idea, so its meaning is chiefly its identification of that individual. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:23. The available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text or enough context to explain anything further about the person. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the surrounding account.

Phaspha is a proper name, rendered also as “Fasfa.” It identifies a named individual or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:38. Since it is a name preserved in the biblical genealogical record, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who or what is being named, rather than describing a broader concept.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “like; fond of”: it expresses personal affection, preference, or warm regard toward someone or something. As a verb, it describes the act of liking or loving rather than naming a person who is loved. It appears 72 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic sense is used across many settings. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something fierce or difficult—harsh, challenging, or hard to face. It can characterize a person, situation, condition, or experience, depending on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, so its central sense is consistent while its specific application depends on context. Its explicit meaning is “fierce; difficult.”

This noun means “palisade,” a barrier or fence formed from upright stakes. It refers to a physical structure rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, across Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. The exact force of the word in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a stake-built barrier or enclosure.

This Greek LXX word means “snow.” It names snow or describes something in relation to snow, functioning as an adjective in its sentences. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, including Psalms, Isaiah, Lamentations, Daniel, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains consistent: snow as a natural substance or visible comparison.

This adjective describes something that can be felt by touch. It points to a tangible or perceptible quality rather than something merely imagined or understood inwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Exodus 10:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the same: something accessible to physical feeling.
